# 45% of remote MCP servers changed their tool definitions in four weeks. The log is now a dataset.

Aleksandr Artamokhov

4 min read

·

Oct 20, 2026

--

Listen

Share

Press enter or click to view image in full size

A client that connects an MCP server reads its tool definitions: names, descriptions and input schemas. The model then reads them as instructions. Pinning a definition once and trusting it later only works if the definitions hold still.

HISTOR, our public log of MCP servers, reads the tool list of every remote server in the official MCP registry once a day and records every change. As of today the whole record is downloadable as files. Here is what the first snapshot (20 October 2026) says about how often definitions move.

## Half of them move

Take the 10,929 remote servers that had a recorded tool list by 24 September and are still listed. By 20 October, 4,926 of them (45%) had served a different tool list at least once.

  * 2,036 changed the description of a tool they already had.

The same files are on Hugging Face and archived on Zenodo, so a paper can cite them: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23512760 for this snapshot.

  * `servers.jsonl.gz`: 83,957 rows (remote endpoints and packages, delisted ones included), with status, tool count and the digest of the current tool list
  * `toolsets.jsonl.gz`: 57,846 tool lists exactly as served, current ones and every one a change replaced
  * `changes.jsonl.gz`: 23,821 changes with tools added, removed and modified, field by field
  * `scans.jsonl.gz` and `pattern-set.json`: WARDEN's pattern matches and the rules
  * `manifest.json`: the SHA-256 of every file, signed by the log's key, with the signed tree head the snapshot was taken under

Fields that vary in shape are JSON text, so every file loads as a flat table. The 45% above is one DuckDB query:
    
    WITH base AS (
      SELECT id FROM 'servers.jsonl.gz'
      WHERE transport <> 'stdio' AND NOT delisted
        AND toolSetDigest IS NOT NULL AND firstPinned <= '2026-09-24T23:59:59Z'
    )
    SELECT count(*) AS servers,
           count(*) FILTER (WHERE id IN (
             SELECT serverId FROM 'changes.jsonl.gz'
             WHERE json_extract_string(summaryJson, '$.detail') = 'full')) AS changed
    FROM base;
    -- 10929 | 4926

To check one server without downloading anything: modelmarket.dev/tools/histor-check.

We build HISTOR and WARDEN. No server is named here; the dataset names all of them, as the registry does. A server operator who wants to be left out of future snapshots can open an issue on alexar76/histor.

Questions or corrections? The discussion is on dev.to.

Why is there no uptime for HISTOR — MCP tool-definition transparency log?

## Александр Артамохов

30 Oct '26

10:51 a.m.

Hello, I would like to request that HISTOR's log be added to the staging witness network, on the 10qps list. vkey histor.modelmarket.dev/log+ad3ca066+AfXpkWqXVW93sChXnhKsNzvGLTFAAredl1jLlEjbr4wU qpd 144 contact alexar76@rambler.ru Origin line: histor.modelmarket.dev/log (equal to the vkey key name). Key type 0x01, Ed25519. Checkpoint: https://histor.modelmarket.dev/checkpoint https://histor.modelmarket.dev/checkpoint Add-checkpoint rate: one request per witness every 10 minutes (144 per day), from a timer on the log's host. The log only grows; consistency proofs are served at https://histor.modelmarket.dev/api/v1/log/proof/consistency?first=&second= https://histor.modelmarket.dev/api/v1/log/proof/consistency?first=&second= and the witness client handles 409 by resubmitting from the witness's size. What it is: HISTOR is a public, append-only log of the tool definitions that MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers listed in the official MCP registry actually serve. Each observation becomes a signed statement, and the statements are leaves of an RFC 9162 Merkle tree (currently about 1.29 million leaves, growing by a few thousand a day). The format is specified at https://github.com/alexar76/histor/blob/main/docs/spec/transparency-log.md https://github.com/alexar76/histor/blob/main/docs/spec/transparency-log.md with test vectors; the checkpoint and note formats were checked byte for byte against golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/note and github.com/transparency-dev/formats/note. Intended users: MCP clients and security tooling that want to check whether the tool definitions they received are the ones the server serves to everyone (split-view detection for tool definitions), and researchers using the weekly open dataset (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23512759). Witness cosignatures are what would turn the log's own signed heads into evidence that it shows everyone the same tree. Load versus utility: 144 add-checkpoint requests per witness per day, small checkpoints, no burst. Expected lifetime: long-lived; the log has run since September 2026 and the origin and key will not change. The same instance also implements c2sp.org/tlog-witness https://histor.modelmarket.dev/witness/v1, https://histor.modelmarket.dev/witness/v1, key histor.modelmarket.dev/witness+87df9f83+BHmgo3SRWlaehFMgWBDIOWFgs1V2YQS+ufBcg/ht6kw/). It is not offered as a network witness yet; if that would be useful once it has run for a while, I would be glad to discuss it separately. Subject: [Dawn] Re: How should we determine the minimum public discovery information?
    
    Hi Chenguang, Two things from running discovery documents and an MCP crawler, and a short answer to your last question. Protocol. "MCP" alone was not enough for us to talk to an endpoint. Since 2026-07-28, MCP servers start a session in one of two incompatible ways. Of the 21,474 remote servers from the official MCP registry that our crawler (HISTOR) has read since 25 October, 4,097 use the new 2026-07-28 way and 17,375 still need initialize. Our own client got the fallback wrong for three days and stopped reading about 2,000 servers it had read on 28 October. So I think 8.2 should say that the protocol comes with a version, or that the binding says how to find it. Freshness. A version number does not tell a client that a description has changed. Between 24 September and 20 October, 81% of the tool definition changes we recorded (17,401 of 21,401) kept the same serverInfo.version. The optional digest on the description endpoint does tell it. That may be worth a sentence next to Freshness. Your elements fit the discovery document in draft-artamokhov-dawn-marketplace-discovery: our "name" is your Display Name, "catalogue_url" is an Endpoint for continuing discovery, "protocol_versions" are its protocols, and "generated_at" is Freshness. The signing key is a Trust Reference outside the minimum, which is how we use it too. # WARDEN — MCP security firewall

Vets what an MCP server says its tools do — tool poisoning, rug pulls, requests for secrets, instructions to send data elsewhere — against static rules, a signed threat feed, origin and tool-definition pinning, before any tool reaches the model. 
One MCP server. Security firewall for advertised tool definitions. Library included.

Transport: stdio (`npx -y @aimarket/warden` / `node dist/mcp-server.js`). Compatible hosts: Claude Desktop, Cursor, Glama, and any MCP client that speaks stdio. No API keys.

Item  | Location
--- | ---
MCP entrypoint (stdio)  | `warden-mcp` → `src/mcp-server.ts`
Tools  | `vet_mcp_server`, `static_scan_tools`, `classify_sensitive_tools`, `check_egress_url`, `canonicalize_json`, `list_scan_rules`, `status_mcp_server`, `approve_mcp_server`, `revoke_mcp_server`
Library  | `import { Warden } from "@aimarket/warden"`
Glama / Docker (stdio)  | `Dockerfile`, `glama.json`
Official MCP Registry  | `server.json` → `io.github.alexar76/warden`

An MCP server tells your agent what its tools do. The agent believes it — that sentence is the attack surface. A tool description is prompt text delivered by a third party straight into your model's context, and a schema field named `api_key` is a request for your secrets phrased as an API.

WARDEN vets a server before any of its tools reach the model, and returns a verdict you can record: allow/block, a 0..1 score, the findings that produced it, a per-tool partition, and the exact rule table that was in force.

Zero npm runtime dependencies. The library's only import is `node:crypto`. The stdio MCP server adds other `node:` builtins (`fs`, `path`, `process`) and still pulls in no packages. It is the firewall out of ARGUS, extracted so you can put it in front of your own MCP host without adopting an agent.

Decimal/NATO secret encodings and MCP Git commit/push now have regressions; the complete 28-case hook replay is a failing local CI/release gate (`npm run test:redteam`).


## Also in the box

  * `EgressGuard` — an outbound allowlist to wrap any request a tool makes. A tool reaching a host you never listed is the classic phone-home tell. `*.example.com` matches subdomains; an empty allowlist blocks everything rather than allowing everything.
  * `isSensitiveTool` / `classifyTools` — glob classification of tools that must require per-call approval. Sensitive tools stay advertised; they just cannot run unattended.
  * `canonicalize` / `parseJsonStrict` — a strict RFC 8785 (JCS) implementation, also exported as `@aimarket/warden/jcs` so another implementation can be byte-checked against it. Integers only beyond `MAX_SAFE_JSON_INTEGER`, refusal (not escaping) on lone surrogates, and a reason code on every refusal.

## ERC-8004 identity

WARDEN is ERC-8004 agent `96684` on Base, registered on 2026-10-01 in the canonical IdentityRegistry `0x8004A169…a432` and owned by the AIMarket operator wallet `0x1218ff36…Ad0a`. Its registration file lists the web page, the npm package and the hosted `warden-scan` endpoint. Transactions and how to check them: ERC-8004 identities.
